stories.headline: GOP accuses Walz allies of burying $52M Medicaid fraud report before election
stories.note: Minnesota Republicans say Walz's Democratic allies are keeping a $52 million Medicaid fraud report under wraps until after the election.
body: Minnesota Republicans say Gov. Tim Walz's administration and Democratic lawmakers kept a state-commissioned Medicaid review away from the Legislature for months. The review flagged more than $52 million in improper payments, and Republicans argue the delay robbed them of a chance to act on its specific findings before the election.

Walz announced the outside review in October 2025, and the state hired Optum to examine 14 high-risk Medicaid services. The report found the improper payments but cautioned they aren't automatically fraud, waste or abuse. The Department of Human Services released a heavily redacted version in February, saying it needed to protect Optum's trade secrets and avoid handing criminals a guide to gaming the system.

GOP state Sen. Jordan Rasmusson tried in April to force the full report into the open, but his amendment failed on a party-line vote. A version of it later passed in May as part of a budget bill that lets a small group of committee members review the report. Requests went in during May and June, yet those lawmakers only got access last week, so any fixes now have to wait until the Legislature returns in January.

House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the Republican nominee for governor, told Fox News Digital, "Fraud here has exploded under the Walz administration," and questioned why the report stayed hidden with the election only four weeks away. Rasmusson, who has now read the unredacted version, said it "underscores the systemic failures of the Walz administration and Minnesota Democrats to protect Minnesota from fraud."

State Sen. John Hoffman, who has also seen the report, pushed back. He argued a report about weak spots in public programs shouldn't be published before those weak spots are fixed, and said it's already outdated because of laws passed this year. DHS says it released the reports last week as the new law requires.

Why it matters: Minnesota's fraud scandals already helped end Walz's re-election bid in January. With the state Senate split 34-33 and the House tied 67-67, Republicans are pressing the case that Democrats sat on fraud findings right before voters decide who controls state government.

stories.headline: Biden-era FBI records reveal sprawling Wiles monitoring as buried contacts surface
stories.note: Declassified records show Biden's FBI tracked at least 39 contacts tied to Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles, more fuel for the weaponization case.
body: Records released Monday by the White House show the Biden-era FBI tracked phone metadata for Susie Wiles, who was then running Donald Trump's political operation and is now his White House chief of staff. From at least February through May 2023, investigators logged who called her, whom she called, when, and for how long.

The logs map Wiles' contacts with at least 21 attorneys, along with campaign staff, Trump Organization employees, two Secret Service officials and reporters from CNN, The Washington Post and Politico. Most entries identify people only by generic labels such as lawyer or campaign. The records don't show what was said or what agents hoped to learn, but in one March 2023 entry investigators logged a 41-second call from one of her lawyers and then went back through earlier calls between the two.

The monitoring was part of the FBI's classified-documents investigation, code-named Plasmic Echo. Then-FBI Director Christopher Wray sought the probe and Attorney General Merrick Garland approved it in March 2022. It led to the Aug. 8, 2022, search of Mar-a-Lago and was later handed to special counsel Jack Smith. The same records show pre-raid checklists asking agents to pin down travel plans for Trump, Melania Trump and Barron Trump.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called Smith's operation "a disgraceful abuse of government power" and said those responsible must be held accountable. Heritage Foundation foreign policy expert Victoria Coates told Fox News Digital the tracking was "unprecedented, dangerous and should be illegal," and contrasted it with how the Justice Department handled President Biden's own classified-documents case.

Why it matters: Reuters reported in February that FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau had subpoenaed his and Wiles' phone records while they were private citizens. These documents show how far that reach went, into a presidential campaign's lawyers, staff and press contacts, and they give Republicans hard evidence for their argument that the Biden Justice Department was weaponized against Trump.

stories.headline: Letitia James' underdog rival turns AG's own playbook against her with scathing 52-count campaign 'indictment'
stories.note: Republican Saritha Komatireddy flipped Tish James' own tactics on her with a 52-count list of alleged failures on hate crimes and fraud.
body: Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican challenging New York Attorney General Letitia James, released a mock 52-count "indictment" of the Democratic incumbent on Thursday, just hours before the two met for their first televised debate.

The document casts James as the defendant and accuses her of neglecting the job of top law enforcement officer: failing to deal with mentally ill people living on the streets, repeat offenders, hate crimes and fraud while focusing on her fights with President Trump. Komatireddy is a former federal prosecutor who won convictions against Islamist terrorists and prosecuted Mexican drug cartel leaders.

One count hits James for not getting a law changed that blocks some rape prosecutions, even with eight legislative sessions under her own party's control. "When a law keeps prosecutors from charging rape, it is the chief law enforcement officer's job to get it changed," Komatireddy wrote.

James' campaign brushed it off as a stunt, saying the attorney general files real lawsuits every day, and pointed to her office's arrest that day of a Queens pharmacy owner accused of a $31 million Medicaid fraud. Komatireddy's campaign answered that James' whole tenure has been a political stunt, and claimed that crime rose 26% and homelessness 38% on her watch while New York ranked last in prosecuting Medicaid fraud.

Why it matters: New York is deep blue, and a Siena poll last month had James ahead 52% to 39%. But her lead shrank by five points between August and September, and the race gives Republicans a stage to turn James' long legal crusade against Trump, including her civil fraud case, into a public-safety argument against her.

stories.headline: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges related to alleged torture of Americans
stories.note: The former Venezuelan dictator and his wife face new charges in Manhattan over the alleged torture of Americans, a win for the Trump administration's tough line.
body: Federal prosecutors in Manhattan were expected to bring new charges against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, over the alleged torture of Americans, according to Fox News' David Spunt and Jake Paronich. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald was set to speak after a 10:30 a.m. court hearing Thursday.

Any new counts would be added to a case that already charges cocaine trafficking, narco-terrorism and weapons offenses. Prosecutors allege Maduro and others helped move thousands of tons of cocaine into the United States, money that funded and supported violent terrorist groups. Maduro and Flores deny the allegations.

Both are trying to get the case thrown out, arguing they're protected by sovereign immunity. Prosecutors say the U.S. hasn't recognized Maduro as Venezuela's head of state since January 2019, and that Venezuela hasn't claimed immunity for them. "The defendants are former rogue officials of a formerly rogue state with no entitlement to immunity," they wrote. Maduro is separately challenging the narco-terrorism count.

Thursday's hearing was originally scheduled to take up Flores' request to be released from custody because of medical problems, including a heart condition. Her lawyers have proposed home confinement with GPS monitoring, round-the-clock armed guards, surrender of her travel documents and a court-approved custodian.

Why it matters: charges tied to the torture of Americans would raise the stakes in the case against the former dictator, and they underline the Trump administration's hard line on Maduro's regime as his lawyers try to get the case dismissed.

stories.headline: Mamdani dined at NYC Palestinian restaurant blasted for 'openly genocidal' menu on Oct. 7 anniversary
stories.note: NYC's Democratic mayor picked the Oct. 7 anniversary to eat at a restaurant accused of an "openly genocidal" menu, another bad look for him.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani had dinner Wednesday night, the third anniversary of Hamas' Oct. 7 attacks on Israel, at Ayat Hinds Hall, a Palestinian restaurant on the Upper West Side, the New York Post reports.

The restaurant is part of a chain whose Brooklyn location drew national criticism in December 2023 for a menu section titled "From the River to the Sea," which critics called "openly genocidal." The Anti-Defamation League considers the slogan an antisemitic call for Israel's destruction. The Upper West Side spot is named after Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in January 2024, and nods to the Columbia University protesters who renamed Hamilton Hall after her.

The owners, Abdul Elenani and Ayat Masoud, said at the time that they weren't calling for Israel to be wiped out. Elenani told the Post the slogan had been on the menu for months before the attacks, said he supports a two-state solution, and condemned violence on both sides.

It isn't clear who the mayor ate with. He had already been heckled and booed by anti-Israel protesters at a vigil for Jewish victims of the Oct. 7 attacks and Palestinians killed in the war that followed. When he left the restaurant, activists waiting outside called him a traitor, and his security team had to hold them back.

Why it matters: on a day meant to honor Jewish victims of terror, the Democrats' highest-profile mayor chose a restaurant chain known for a slogan the ADL calls antisemitic, and he still couldn't satisfy the far-left protesters who now accuse him of betraying their cause.

stories.headline: Abdul El-Sayed's long history of trashing Obama resurfaces ahead of rally with former prez
stories.note: Michigan's Democratic Senate hopeful is about to rally with Obama after years of trashing him, an awkward split for Democrats.
body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, is scheduled to rally with Barack Obama in Detroit on Oct. 24. But years of El-Sayed knocking Obama as not progressive enough have resurfaced ahead of the event, the New York Post reports, drawing on a timeline compiled by CNN.

In a 2012 HuffPost piece written right after Obama won re-election, El-Sayed wrote, "Obama was not the right choice — he just wasn't the wrong one." He accused Obama of continuing wars, violating civil liberties and deporting record numbers of people, argued the country wasn't better off, and called Obamacare a watered-down bill that bent to healthcare lobbyists.

The criticism kept coming. During his failed 2017 run for Michigan governor, he told Vox that Obama's policies were centrist and middle-of-the-road. In January 2020, at a University of Chicago panel, he warned Democrats not to repeat the mistakes of the Obama years and argued that Obama never changed the structure of the economy, which set the stage for Trump.

Today El-Sayed tells crowds that Obama's 2008 win was the first time he saw himself reflected in politics. In a statement to CNN, he said Obama "changed what was possible for someone like me, with a name like mine," and said he can't wait to tell him so later this month. His campaign and Obama's representatives didn't respond to the Post.

Why it matters: El-Sayed is in a tight race with Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. He has also drawn criticism from Jewish and Black groups over his focus on Israel and Gaza, and he campaigned with Kamala Harris last month despite backing the 2024 Uncommitted movement against her. His record of attacking Obama hands Rogers fresh material and shows how far left Michigan Democrats' nominee really is.

stories.headline: GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson slams Dem Josh Turek for missing most votes in Iowa Legislature: 'You stole from taxpayers'
stories.note: Hinson is hammering her Democratic opponent in the Iowa Senate race for missing most of his votes as a state lawmaker.
body: Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) went after her Democratic opponent, state Rep. Josh Turek, for his attendance record in the Iowa Legislature during their U.S. Senate debate Wednesday.

Hinson said Turek failed to show up for 58% of votes this year, including the Iowa Farm Bill, and called him one of the most absent and most liberal members when he did vote. Anyone in the private sector with that record, she said, wouldn't get a promotion. They'd get fired.

Turek fired back that Hinson has missed 193 votes in Congress, voted for healthcare cuts in a state facing healthcare and cancer crises, and collected about $50,000 through a $178-a-day federal per diem for House members on top of her salary, despite being a multimillionaire.

Hinson was ready. She noted that Iowa has the same kind of per diem for state lawmakers and that Turek took all of it while skipping votes. "So you took the per diem. You stole from taxpayers. You should refund that money," she told him. Hinson says Turek collected $20,000 through the program.

Why it matters: the Iowa race is one of the most closely watched in the country and could decide which party controls the Senate starting in January 2027. Turek leads by just 1 point in the RealClearPolitics polling average, and the no-show attack gives Hinson a simple pocketbook contrast to close the gap.
